description: We’re a team of students driven by technology, innovation, and complex challenges. With a shared background in Systems Engineering, each member brings a unique set of skills and perspectives to the table. We thrive on learning, collaboration, and creative problem-solving. We’re jumping into this hackathon ready to experiment, contribute, and see just how far we can go together.
summary:
AstroTwin helps astronauts check their own health on long missions, when Mission Control can be more than 20 minutes away. It shows the crew member's body as a clickable 3D digital twin. Each body system is green, amber or red, with an icon and a word so it reads at a glance. When something turns red, the astronaut taps it and an AI copilot explains what the result means, how spaceflight affects it and what to do next, including when to call the flight surgeon.

The tool follows the five hazards of human spaceflight defined by NASA's Human Research Program: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment. A daily routine with points and streaks turns measurements into part of the mission schedule. Real blood test data from the Inspiration4 crew, taken from NASA's Open Science Data Repository, shows how the body changes before and after flight.

AstroTwin runs offline in a single web page. The same engine can help community health workers in remote Andean villages in Peru, many of them hours from the nearest clinic, decide when someone needs to be referred.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A crew member on the way to Mars cannot wait 20 minutes for an answer from Earth, and most of them are not doctors. AstroTwin gives them three answers: how they are doing, what a result means, and what to do now.

The body appears as a holographic 3D twin. Heart, kidneys and hydration, bones, brain and sleep, immune defenses, mood and a radiation shell are all clickable. Each one opens a panel with its function, current status, a trend chart and clear actions.

Every indicator uses a traffic light: green, amber or red, always with an icon and a word, so color-blind users can read it too. For example, systolic blood pressure under 120 is green, 120 to 139 is amber, and 140 or more is red. Sleep of 7 hours or more is green, 6 to 7 is amber, and under 6 is red. The modules affect each other the way the body does: a bad night of sleep raises blood pressure and lowers mood, and drinking too little water also raises blood pressure.

The AI copilot explains each result in plain language and gives concrete steps. It always says why ("your blood pressure has risen for three days and you slept 4.5 hours"), and it says when a result needs the crew or the flight surgeon on the ground. We built it on explainable rules on purpose, because a crew member should be able to see the reason behind any health advice.

Daily missions turn health tasks into part of the schedule: measure, drink water, exercise, sleep, and take shelter during a solar storm. They give points, streaks and levels.

A demo panel lets you trigger a solar storm, a bad night, low water intake or high blood pressure. You can also switch the destination between low Earth orbit, the Moon and Mars, which changes the radiation baseline and the communication delay.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

Each module is linked to one of the five hazards of human spaceflight from NASA's Human Research Program, so the astronaut can see which hazard is behind each risk.

The "real flight data" section uses blood tests of the four Inspiration4 crew members from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569 and OSD-575): 13 blood markers at seven time points, from 92 days before launch to 194 days after landing. We cleaned the files into a table of 1,084 rows and dropped 14 rows marked as unreliable. A heat map shows which values left the reference range, a chart follows each marker over time, and a short summary says what changed with flight.

HOW IT WORKS

AstroTwin is one HTML file that works with no internet connection. We wrote it in JavaScript, used Three.js for the 3D twin and esbuild to bundle it. All data stays on the device. Vital signs, sleep, radiation, hydration, exercise and mood are simulated within realistic ranges, and the interface labels them as simulated. Only the Inspiration4 blood data is real. We cleaned the data with Python and pandas and tested the interface with Playwright.

IMPACT ON EARTH

Peru's high Andes have the same problem as a crew on the way to Mars: help is far away, equipment is scarce and the connection is unreliable. According to Gestión (2025), 760 districts have no health facility with basic care and a lab, 718 of them rural, and more than 1.5 million people travel from 50 minutes to over three hours to reach one. Peru's Ministry of Health reported 19,108 pneumonia episodes in children under five through the first 34 weeks of 2026, with 94 deaths. In Cusco, most pneumonia deaths during frost season are adults over 60.



Acting early makes a difference. In Cusco, the share of child pneumonia deaths that happened outside a hospital fell from 76% in 2023 to 33.3% in 2025, as more families sought care before the illness got worse. The Ministry of Health already tells families to take a child with fever, cough, fast breathing or loss of appetite to the nearest health center right away. Peru also has more than 35,000 community health agents, and they are often the first people to see these signs.

Our community mode puts the same engine in their hands. It uses a high-contrast light theme and large buttons, and it works with few or no sensors. The agent marks what they see, such as fast breathing, a child who cannot drink, or a cold home, and the copilot gives one of three outcomes: handle it here, watch and re-check, or refer to the clinic. A referral comes with a printable sheet. When data is missing, the copilot is more cautious and refers earlier. Its thresholds are examples and must be checked against Ministry of Health protocols before any real use.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

AstroTwin turns health data into a body you can touch. A crew member sees which part of the 3D twin changed color, taps it, and gets the reason and the next step, all without a connection to Earth.

The body systems affect each other in the app as they do in real life. A bad night of sleep pushes blood pressure up and mood down, so the astronaut can see how one habit spreads to other parts of the body instead of reading separate numbers. The copilot always explains its advice with the data behind it, and the daily missions add points and streaks so that routine health checks feel like part of the mission schedule.

The same engine adapts to where it is used. Switching the destination from orbit to the Moon or Mars changes the radiation baseline and the communication delay. In community mode, the same design works in an Andean village with a light, high-contrast theme and few or no sensors, and it becomes more cautious when data is missing.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

AstroTwin is a prototype and does not diagnose. Its rules are not clinically validated. Next, we want to train an anomaly detection model on open physiological data so the tool learns each person's normal values, connect real wearable sensors, review the rules with flight surgeons and Peruvian health staff, and test it with a small pilot group.

AI USE

We used Claude (Anthropic) to help with research, code, data cleaning, text and the demo video. The team reviewed and tested every part. The demo video carries a visible "AI-assisted video" watermark, and the README notes which code was AI-assisted.

The Team Behind AstroTwin

Rodrigo Estefanero — Team Lead and Lead Developer (Peru)

Coordinates the team and owns the product from idea to submission. Built the AstroTwin app, including the 3D digital twin, the health dashboard and the real flight data panel, and connected every module to the traffic light and the copilot. Also directed the demo video and the final project story.

Sergio Estrada — Data Analyst and Data Engineer (Peru)

Collected and cleaned the project's clinical and NASA datasets and researched the treatments behind the copilot's advice. Selected the variables that matter for monitoring, such as vital signs, neurological status and key lab tests, removed impossible values and merged everything into ready-to-use tables. His clean data is the base the app reads from.

Emanuel Hilacondo — AI Copilot Developer (Peru)

Works on the copilot, the part of AstroTwin that talks to the astronaut. Shaped the rules and responses that explain what each result means and how spaceflight affects it. Helped define when the crew member can act alone and when to alert the crew or the flight surgeon.

Renzo Mamani — UI/UX Designer (Peru)

Designed the interface and the path a crew member follows through each screen. Focused on making every status readable at a glance, with color always paired with an icon and a word. His goal was a screen that someone without medical training can understand in seconds.

Brayan Auccacusi — Research and Project Planning (Peru)

Researched the challenge and the NASA resources behind it, then turned the team's ideas into one shared plan. Kept the task list that organized the hackathon and helped decide what to build first. His research defined the problem AstroTwin sets out to solve.

Alberth Riveros — Deployment and Version Control (Peru)

Manages the project's GitHub repository and the deployment of the AstroTwin website. Set up the public page so judges and users can open the app from any browser with a single link. Keeps the code organized, tracks changes from the whole team and makes sure the live version matches the latest work.
